questions.q: What surprised Thurston about native Nigerians' reaction to his name?
a: They sometimes accepted it less readily than white people
They pronounced it more accurately than his teachers
They assumed it was a nickname he chose
They asked him to change it at school
questions.why: Lesson one says a Nigerian friend's father lectured him about the name, showing more resistance than he got from white people.

questions.q: What does the term Oreo mean in the book?
a: A Black person seen as white inside for having white friends
A white person who adopts Black culture
A Black student who hides his grades
A mixed-race person who fits neither group
questions.why: Lesson two explains that the insult described a Black person who spent time with white kids and was thought to be rejecting his race.

questions.q: What does Thurston say cross-racial friendships can do?
a: Build trust and help both communities understand each other
Prove that race no longer matters in society
Replace the need for antiracist policies
Make Black students adopt white habits faster
questions.why: Lesson two argues genuine friendships give both groups insights they could not get inside their own cultural bubbles.

questions.q: What did colleagues assume about Thurston's views on President Obama?
a: That he spoke for all Black people
That he opposed Obama's policies
That he had worked on the campaign
That he knew Obama personally
questions.why: Lesson three says coworkers expected him to deliver a single black community stance on the president.

questions.q: What is black denial, as Thurston uses the term?
a: Black people rejecting their race and shared experience
White people refusing to admit their privilege
Students avoiding discussions about slavery
Companies denying they discriminate at work
questions.why: Lesson three describes colleagues who refused to acknowledge their blackness and therefore felt no solidarity with him.
